title: Patient assessment & medical history
blurb: Medical, social and dental history, the extra-oral and intra-oral examination, and the dental nurse's part in each.
question: A patient arrives for an extraction. Their medical history form was last updated three years ago, and while chatting they mention they now take 'a blood thinner'. What should happen before treatment starts, and why does it matter?

teach.body: Before any treatment, the dentist needs to know who they are treating: their health, medicines, lifestyle and dental worries. This is the patient assessment. Its purpose is to spot anything that could make treatment unsafe, change how it is done, or point to disease. The dentist examines and diagnoses. Your job is to support: hand out and check forms, prepare the instruments, record findings exactly as called, and keep everything confidential.

steps.label: Presenting complaint
steps.sub: Why the patient has come in today

teach.caption: Dental nurses do not diagnose or plan treatment (GDC Scope of Practice). You record and support each step.

teach.h: The medical history: checked every time
teach.body: The patient (or parent or carer) completes a written medical history form, which the dentist then checks with them verbally. It is signed and dated. It must be updated at every new course of treatment and confirmed before surgery, because health and medicines change. If a history is out of date, the patient confirms or updates it BEFORE treatment. Important findings are flagged as a medical alert in the record.

teach.h: What the history picks up, and why it matters
head: Finding
Why it matters chairside
rows: Bleeding after extractions; recent INR needed
Risk of jaw bone necrosis after extractions
Seizure or attack; have medicines ready
Affects timing, radiographs and some drugs
teach.caption: The dentist decides what changes. You make sure the form is complete, signed and flagged, and pass on anything new the patient tells you.

teach.h: Which history does it belong to?

rows.label: Past treatment, anxiety, problems with LA

teach.note: Smoking and alcohol matter because they raise the risk of gum disease and oral cancer.

teach.caption: The lateral borders of the tongue and the floor of the mouth are high-risk sites for oral cancer, so they are checked carefully.

teach.h: The BPE: a quick gum screen
teach.caption: The Basic Periodontal Examination uses a WHO probe (0.5 mm ball, black band 3.5–5.5 mm). The highest score in each of six sextants is recorded.

items: Check the medical history form is complete, signed and dated, and up to date.
Lay out the kit: mouth mirror, probe, WHO BPE probe, tweezers and the patient's chart.
Seat and position the patient; give safety glasses and a bib.
Record each finding exactly as the dentist calls it, at the right tooth or site.
Flag medical alerts and tell the dentist about anything new the patient mentions.
Keep the record secure and confidential.

teach.text: 'The patient said nothing has changed' is not enough if the form is years old. An out-of-date history must be confirmed or updated by the patient and checked by the dentist BEFORE treatment, especially before surgery.

items: Purpose: identify risks that affect safe treatment, and spot disease.
Medical history: written, checked verbally, signed and dated; updated every course of treatment and before surgery.
Key flags: anticoagulants, bisphosphonates, allergies, heart disease, diabetes, epilepsy, asthma, pregnancy.
Extra-oral: face, lymph nodes, TMJ. Intra-oral: soft tissues, teeth, gums, BPE.
The dentist diagnoses; the nurse records, supports and keeps it confidential.

summary: You can now explain why a full medical history is taken and kept up to date, link common findings to chairside risks, describe what the extra-oral and intra-oral examinations check, outline the BPE, and set out the dental nurse's role within the GDC scope of practice.

A.q: You notice a patient's medical history has not been updated for three years. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Assume nothing has changed and proceed
Have the patient update it before treatment
Update the form yourself from the old records
Postpone the appointment for six months
A.why: Health and medicines change. The patient must confirm and update the history, and the dentist check it, before treatment.

whyNot.0: Assuming nothing has changed could miss a new medicine or condition that makes treatment unsafe.
whyNot.2: Only the patient can tell you what has changed; old records can't.
whyNot.3: There's no need to postpone; updating the form usually takes a few minutes.

A.q: Which medicine on a medical history form would most concern the dentist before an extraction because of bleeding?
options: Metformin
Salbutamol
Warfarin
Levothyroxine
A.why: Warfarin is an anticoagulant, so bleeding after an extraction may be prolonged. The dentist will want a recent INR result.

whyNot.0: Metformin treats type 2 diabetes; it doesn't affect clotting.
whyNot.1: Salbutamol is an asthma reliever inhaler.
whyNot.3: Levothyroxine treats an underactive thyroid and doesn't increase bleeding.

A.q: During a BPE, the black band of the probe is partly visible in the deepest pocket of a sextant. Which code is recorded?
options: Code 1
Code 2
Code 4
Code 3
A.why: Code 3 means a probing depth of 3.5–5.5 mm: the black band is partly hidden.

whyNot.0: Code 1 is bleeding on probing with the black band fully visible.
whyNot.1: Code 2 is calculus or an overhang with the black band fully visible.
whyNot.2: Code 4 is when the black band disappears completely (over 5.5 mm).

B.q: A patient asks why they must fill in a medical history again at every course of treatment. What is the best explanation?
options: It is needed for the practice's insurance policy
Their health and medicines may have changed
The old form will have been shredded
It helps the dentist charge the right fee
B.why: New illnesses, medicines or allergies can change how treatment is carried out safely, so the history is updated each time.

whyNot.0: The purpose is patient safety, not insurance.
whyNot.2: Records are kept for years (11 years for dental records); the form is updated because health changes.
whyNot.3: Fees are not decided by the medical history.

B.q: Which of these is part of the EXTRA-oral examination?
options: Feeling the lymph nodes in the neck
Recording a BPE score for each sextant
Checking the floor of the mouth
Charting existing fillings
B.why: Extra-oral means outside the mouth: face, skin, lips, lymph nodes and the TMJ.

whyNot.1: The BPE is part of the intra-oral examination of the gums.
whyNot.2: The floor of the mouth is checked during the intra-oral soft tissue examination.
whyNot.3: Charting the teeth is done during the intra-oral examination.

B.q: A patient's history shows they take a bisphosphonate (alendronic acid). Why might this matter for an extraction?
options: It makes local anaesthetic wear off faster
It causes the patient to faint easily
It stains the teeth during treatment
It increases the risk of jaw bone necrosis
B.why: Bisphosphonates and other antiresorptive drugs carry a risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw after extractions, so the dentist plans accordingly.

whyNot.0: Bisphosphonates don't affect how long local anaesthetic lasts.
whyNot.1: Fainting isn't a known effect of bisphosphonates.
whyNot.2: Staining is linked to drugs like tetracycline, not bisphosphonates.

C.q: What is the main purpose of taking a medical history before dental treatment?
options: To identify risks to safe treatment
To decide which dentist the patient will see
To check the patient is registered with a GP
To work out how long the appointment should take
C.why: The medical history shows conditions, medicines and allergies that could make treatment unsafe or need it to be adapted.

whyNot.1: Which dentist the patient sees is an appointment decision.
whyNot.2: GP details may be recorded, but that isn't the main purpose.
whyNot.3: Appointment length depends on the treatment, not the history.

C.q: During a new-patient examination, which task is within the dental nurse's role?
options: Deciding which teeth need fillings
Diagnosing gum disease from the BPE
Recording findings exactly as called
Choosing which radiographs to take
C.why: The nurse records findings accurately. Diagnosis and treatment planning belong to the dentist under the GDC Scope of Practice.

whyNot.0: Deciding treatment is treatment planning, which dental nurses don't do.
whyNot.1: Interpreting the BPE into a diagnosis is the dentist's job.
whyNot.3: Justifying radiographs is the dentist's (IR(ME)R practitioner's) role.

C.q: During the soft tissue examination, which area is a high-risk site for oral cancer that is checked carefully?
options: The hard palate behind the incisors
The lateral border of the tongue
The attached gingiva of upper molars
The incisal edges of the lower incisors
C.why: The lateral borders of the tongue and the floor of the mouth are the commonest sites for oral cancer.

whyNot.0: The hard palate is examined but is not one of the highest-risk sites.
whyNot.2: The attached gingiva is examined but is a lower-risk site.
whyNot.3: Incisal edges are tooth surfaces, not soft tissue.

reteach.title: Think of a pilot's pre-flight check
reteach.question: A pilot runs the same checklist before every flight, however many times they have flown the plane. Why does a dental team check the medical history before every course of treatment?

blocks.body: The plane may be the same, but the weather, the fuel and the load change. The patient may be the same, but their medicines, illnesses and allergies may have changed since you last saw them. A pre-flight check finds problems on the ground, not in the air. A medical history check finds risks before the drill is running or the tooth is out. The dentist is the captain who decides; you help run the checklist and write down the answers.

children.edge: Out of date or patient mentions a change

blocks.text: The BPE, charting and soft tissue checks are INTRA-oral. Lymph nodes, face and TMJ are EXTRA-oral.

explain.body: A written form completed by the patient, checked verbally by the dentist, signed and dated. It is updated at every course of treatment and confirmed before surgery. Out of date? The patient updates it before treatment.

test.q: Before a planned surgical extraction, why is the medical history checked again?
options: To update the patient's address
To meet an IR(ME)R radiography rule
To confirm the appointment fee
To identify risks to safe treatment
test.why: Surgery carries risks such as bleeding and infection, so any new medicine or condition must be known first.

whyNot.0: Contact details matter, but they aren't why the medical history is checked.
whyNot.1: Radiography rules don't require the medical history check before surgery.
whyNot.2: Fees are separate from the medical history.

explain.body: Anticoagulants mean bleeding risk. Bisphosphonates mean a risk of jaw bone necrosis after extraction. Allergies mean avoiding the trigger. Angina, diabetes, epilepsy and asthma mean medical emergency risks, so the right medicines must be ready.

test.q: A patient's history states a latex allergy. Which preparation is most important?
options: Use latex-free gloves and dam
Book a longer appointment
Give the patient an antihistamine
Use only plain local anaesthetic
test.why: Avoiding contact with the allergen is the key step: latex-free gloves, rubber dam and other items.

whyNot.1: Appointment length doesn't prevent a reaction.
whyNot.2: You don't give medicines routinely; avoidance is the answer.
whyNot.3: Latex allergy isn't a reason to change the anaesthetic.

explain.body: Extra-oral: face, skin, lips, lymph nodes and TMJ. Intra-oral: all soft tissues (cheeks, tongue, floor of mouth, palate), then teeth, gums (BPE), bite and plaque. Suspicious findings are recorded and the dentist decides on referral.

left.label: Extra-oral
items: Lymph nodes
TMJ
Face

right.label: Intra-oral
items: Tongue
BPE
Charting

both.label: Both
items: Lips
Swelling
Colour change

test.q: The dentist asks the patient to open and close while feeling just in front of their ears. What is being examined?
options: The parotid duct opening
The submandibular lymph nodes
The temporomandibular joint
The hard palate
test.why: Feeling in front of the ears during opening and closing checks the TMJ for clicking, pain and restricted movement.

whyNot.0: The parotid duct opens inside the cheek, opposite the upper second molar.
whyNot.1: Submandibular nodes are felt under the lower jaw.
whyNot.3: The hard palate is examined inside the mouth.
